title: Monolithic printed-circuit board RF-trap for electrons
authors: Zijue Luo, Jae Eu, Tianyi Wang, Boerge Hemmerling
abstract: Qubits encoded in the spin of trapped electrons have been proposed as a promising novel platform for quantum information processing. While trapping of electrons has been largely carried out in Penning traps for precision measurement purposes, it is desirable to use linear Paul traps instead, leaning on the successes of trapped ion quantum processors. Here we present a Paul trap for electrons made of a single printed circuit board. Our approach requires no assembly and the rigid design minimizes manufacturing intolerances. We characterize the trap performance and observe trapped electron lifetimes of 2.13 ms and secular frequencies of up to 90 MHz.
summary: The paper reports the successful realization of an electron Paul trap fabricated entirely on a monolithic printed circuit board (PCB). This novel design provides mechanical stability for trapping electrons, which serve as qubits. The experiment characterized the trap's performance by measuring lifetimes and determining high secular frequencies using RF/DC field analysis.
main_problem: The goal is to develop a practical, scalable platform for quantum information processing using qubits encoded in trapped electron spins, moving away from traditional Penning traps.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated trapping electrons on a monolithic PCB Paul trap, achieving measurable lifetimes of 2.13 ms and high secular frequencies up to 90 MHz.
method: The experiment involves fabricating the trap entirely on a single printed circuit board (PCB) and characterizing electron confinement using RF/DC electric fields and measuring decay rates.
model_or_system: The physical system is an electron Paul trap built monolithically on a PCB substrate, utilizing both RF pseudopotentials for radial confinement and DC electrodes for axial confinement. The trapping potential depth was characterized to be around 0.6 eV.
key_observables: Trapped electron lifetime ($	au = 2.13$ ms), secular frequencies ($\omega_x \approx 2\pi 	imes 158$ MHz, $\omega_y \approx 2\pi 	imes 161$ MHz), and motional frequency resonances.
important_parameters: RF drive frequency ($\Omega_{	ext{rf}} = 2\pi 	imes 1.732$ GHz), trap depths ($0.59-0.68$ eV), and vacuum pressure ($\approx 5 	imes 10^{-8}$ Torr).
main_assumptions: The short lifetime is attributed to field imperfections, lack of active cooling, and difficulty compensating excess micromotion compared to ion traps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 3D model of the PCB trap structure, finite-element simulations showing pseudopotentials and calculated frequencies, and experimental setups detailing signal generation for lifetime and motional frequency measurements.
paper_structure: The paper details the design of a monolithic Paul trap on a PCB, presents characterization results including measured electron lifetimes and spectral fitting to determine axial and radial secular frequencies by varying DC potentials and RF power.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware engineering challenges in quantum computing platforms. Using a single-PCB approach significantly enhances scalability and robustness compared to complex multi-component traps, making it highly relevant for solid-state or chip-based AMO quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) 3D model of the printed circuit board electron trap. The RF signal for the Paul trap is delivered to the board by an SMA-connected feedline (left side of the board), which is capacitively coupled to an on-board RF resonator. Electrons are trapped near the end of the resonator, at the center of the elongated plated slit. The DC signals are delivered by a D-sub connector (right side of board). (b) Zoomed view of the slit. The numbers 01 to 10 denote the DC electrodes on the top layer; a set of identical electrodes, 11 to 20, is located on the bottom layer. The slit is surrounded by a plated sidewall and a metal annular ring. (c) Schematics of the top (red) and bottom (blue) layers...

FIG. 3. Experimental apparatus. The PCB Paul trap is mounted at the center of a UHV vacuum chamber, with the calcium oven (not visible), copper mesh, and microchannel plate detector arranged along the adjacent viewport axes.

FIG. 2. Finite-element simulation of trap. (a) Pseudopo- tential along the ˆx-axis (perpendicular to the trap board) and (b) along the ˆy-axis (along the slit width). The fitted secular frequencies are ωx = 2π × 157.6 MHz, ωy = 2π × 161.2 MHz, and the trap depths are Ux = 0.59 eV and Uy = 0.68 eV. All simulations assume an RF input power of 36 dBm.

FIG. 4. Schematic diagram of the experiment. The oven provides a thermal beam of calcium atoms, which are photoionized to produce trappable electrons. The Paul trap is driven at 1.732 GHz. Further details are explained in the main text.
FIG. 5. Trapped electron lifetime measurement. The data is fitted with an exponential decay, which yields a life- time of 2.13 ms.
